logline: In a brutally stratified future Brazil, only 3 percent of young people from the impoverished Inland will pass a lethal Process and gain entry to the privileged Offshore - and every candidate has a reason to cheat.

renewal.note: Season 4, released August 14, 2020, concluded the series. Netflix did not renew for a fifth season; creator Pedro Aguilera confirmed the story reached its intended conclusion.

bollymeter.basis: Season 1 holds 85% on Rotten Tomatoes from 20 critics. The Guardian praised its compulsive viewing quality; IndieWire awarded a B+ and called it surprising and impressive. IMDb series rating sits at 7.2 from roughly 30,000 votes.

pull_quotes.text: What it lacks in production dollars it makes up for in the compulsive viewing stakes.
3% features unique elements and compelling characters, plus a strong take on the social implications of the premise.

seasons.review_body: Season 1, Netflix's first Brazilian original, arrived November 2016 directed by Oscar-nominated cinematographer Cesar Charlone. Critics scored it 85 percent on Rotten Tomatoes from 20 reviews, with the consensus crediting its focus on characters with complicated backstories rather than the survival spectacle alone. The Guardian found it compulsive despite modest production values; IndieWire gave it a B+, calling it surprising and impressive. The dystopian frame drew inevitable Hunger Games comparisons but the show's real interest was in the moral calculus of selection - what it does to people when a system tells them scarcity is natural and meritocracy is fair. Bianca Comparato's Michele became the season's moral centre, the candidate who most clearly saw the Process for what it was.

episode_reviews.title: Chapter 01: Plastic
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The premiere drops the audience into The Process with no exposition hand-holding - the rules become clear through the candidates' experience, not a narrator. The first challenge immediately establishes that the show is interested in why people participate, not just whether they survive.
episode_reviews.the_moment: The first elimination in the opening round signals that 3% will not protect anyone the viewer has started to like.

critic_note.text: The characters are the show's strongest point - it skillfully introduces the six core candidates throughout the preliminary challenges.

episode_reviews.title: Chapter 08: Corridor
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The season finale arrives at a genuinely unsettling conclusion that refuses the comfortable resolution of most dystopian narratives. The question of whether reaching the Offshore was ever worth the cost hangs over every choice the finale makes.
episode_reviews.the_moment: Michele's final decision in the Process - the moment that defines the series' moral argument about complicity and survival.

bollymeter.basis: Season 2 climbed to 89% on Rotten Tomatoes from 3 critics. Decider's Kayla Cobb wrote that by blowing up its own premise the show finally lived up to its lofty ambitions. The pivot from survival competition to resistance movement was widely praised.

pull_quotes.text: By blowing up its own premise and becoming a show about the morality of revolution, 3% is finally living up to its own lofty ambitions.
3% doesn't offer solutions, but it does showcase characters challenging the basic idea that some should have more than others.

seasons.review_body: Season 2 arrived April 2018 with a structural gamble: blowing up the Process framework that defined Season 1 and expanding the show's world to include the Offshore itself and the Cause, the resistance movement seeking to dismantle the selection system entirely. Critics approved at 89 percent, though from only 3 reviews. IndieWire's Liz Shannon Miller appreciated the show's willingness to question whether revolution can be moral when it uses the same violence it opposes. Decider called it the season where the series finally lived up to its ambitions. The expanded episode count (8 to 10) allowed the Offshore society to be depicted with the same critical lens the Process had received in Season 1.
seasons.season_over_season: Pivoting from competition drama to political thriller, Season 2 gained thematic scope at the cost of the survival-pressure momentum that drove Season 1.

bollymeter.basis: Season 3 received no formal critic score on Rotten Tomatoes, indicating limited critical coverage. Audience scores remained solid. The Shell - an alternative community - was introduced as a third faction, expanding the political triangle.

seasons.review_body: Season 3, released June 2019, introduced the Shell as a third social formation beyond the Inland and the Offshore, a move that gave the series a more genuinely triangulated political argument. Critical tracking was sparse - Rotten Tomatoes logged no formal reviews - but audience reception remained consistent with the prior seasons. The Shell storyline complicated the revolution-versus-system binary that Season 2 had established, asking whether an alternative community built on different principles was possible or whether every power structure inevitably reproduces the one it replaced. The eight-episode count matched Season 1's disciplined brevity after Season 2's expansion.
seasons.season_over_season: The Shell faction introduces a genuine third option in the show's political argument - Season 3 is the most philosophically ambitious, if less immediately gripping.

bollymeter.basis: The finale season logged 80% on Rotten Tomatoes though with fewer than 50 audience ratings tracked. The shortened 7-episode final run concluded the series' arc with the resolution the political argument had been building toward.

seasons.review_body: Season 4, the final run of seven episodes released August 2020, closed out a four-year run that established 3% as one of the most politically honest dystopian dramas in the streaming era. The finale resolved the series' central argument about whether the 3 percent selection was ever reformable or required dismantling entirely - and did so without flinching from the cost of the answer. The truncated episode count felt appropriately compressed for a show reaching its conclusion. The overall series leaves a distinctive imprint: a low-budget Brazilian production that consistently outperformed its resources because it understood that its premise was an economic allegory, not a game show.
seasons.season_over_season: The compressed 7-episode finale resolves four seasons of political conflict without the sentimentality that mars most dystopian series endings.
